[[File:Albertson index.svg|thumb|The vertices are labeled by their [[degree (graph theory)|degree]], and the edges by their '''imbalance''', the difference of the degrees of the vertices [[incidence (graph)|incident]] to them. The '''Albertson index''' <math>\operatorname{Alb}(G)</math> of a graph <math>G</math> is the sum of the imbalances of all edges.]]

The '''Albertson index''' (also known as '''irregularity''' or '''Albertson irregularity index''') is a [[graph invariant]] that measures the irregularity of a [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] by summing the imbalances of all its edges. It was introduced by [[Michael O. Albertson]] in 1997 as a single parameter to capture how "non-regular" a graph is.<ref name="albertson1997">{{cite journal |last=Albertson |first=Michael O. |title=The irregularity of a graph |journal=Ars Combinatoria |year=1997 |volume=46 |pages=219–225 |url=https://combinatorialpress.com/article/ars/Volume%20046/volume-46-paper-16.pdf}}</ref>

== Definition ==

For a [[simple graph|simple]] [[undirected graph]] <math>G = (V, E)</math>, the '''imbalance''' of an edge <math>e = {u,v}</math> is defined as:
:<math>\operatorname{imb}(e) = |\deg(u) - \deg(v)|</math>
where <math>\deg(u)</math> and <math>\deg(v)</math> denote the [[degree (graph theory)|degrees]] of vertices <math>u</math> and <math>v</math>.

The '''Albertson index''' of <math>G</math>, denoted <math>\operatorname{Alb}(G)</math> (sometimes <math>\operatorname{I}(G)</math> or <math>\operatorname{irr}(G)</math> in the literature), is the sum of the imbalances of all edges:
:<math>\operatorname{Alb}(G) = \sum_{uv \in E(G)} |\deg(u) - \deg(v)|</math>
A graph is [[regular graph|regular]] if and only if its Albertson index is zero.

== Properties and bounds ==

The Albertson index is always an [[even and odd|even]] integer. For a graph with <math>n</math> vertices, the index is bounded by <math>O(n^3)</math>.<ref name="albertson1997"/>

=== Maximum irregularity ===

The maximum Albertson index over all graphs with <math>n</math> vertices is less than <math>\frac{4n^3}{27}</math>, and this bound is tight. The extremal graphs that approach this bound are of the form <math>H_{r,n} = K_r \vee \overline{K}{n-r}</math>, the [[join (graph theory)|join]] of a [[complete graph]] <math>K_r</math> and an [[independent set (graph theory)|independent set]] <math>\overline{K}{n-r}</math>, where <math>r</math> is approximately <math>n/3</math>.<ref name="albertson1997"/>

A graph <math>G</math> is called '''critical''' if adding or removing any single edge does not increase its Albertson index. Albertson proved that a graph is critical if and only if it is of the form <math>H_{r,n}</math> for some <math>r \leq \frac{n}{3}</math>, a result used to establish the general upper bound.<ref name="albertson1997"/>

For specific classes of graphs, tighter bounds exist:

If <math>G</math> is [[bipartite graph|bipartite]], then 
:<math>\operatorname{Alb}(G) \leq \frac{2n^3}{27}</math>. 
The irregularity of a [[complete bipartite graph]] <math>K_{t,n-t}</math> is <math>t(n-t)(n-2t)</math>.

If <math>G</math> is [[triangle-free graph|triangle-free]], then 
:<math>\operatorname{Alb}(G) < \frac{4n^3}{27}</math>.

=== Extremal trees ===

Among all [[tree (graph theory)|trees]] with <math>n</math> vertices, the Albertson index is bounded by:
:<math>2 \leq \operatorname{Alb}(T) \leq (n-1)(n-2)</math>
The lower bound of 2 is achieved exclusively by the [[path graph]] <math>P_n</math>, while the upper bound is achieved exclusively by the [[star graph]] <math>K_{1,n-1}</math>.<ref name="albertson1997"/>

=== Minimal irregularity ===

While the star graph maximizes irregularity for trees, the minimal irregularity for certain graph classes has also been studied. For a connected graph <math>G</math> with <math>k</math> [[pendant vertex|pendant vertices]], a general lower bound is <math>\operatorname{Alb}(G) \geq 2k</math>.<ref name="retietal2022">{{cite journal |last1=Réti |first1=Tamás |last2=Ghorbani |first2=Maryam |last3=Dehmer |first3=Matthias |last4=Emmert-Streib |first4=Frank |title=Irregularity of graphs |journal=MATCH Communications in Mathematical and in Computer Chemistry |year=2022 |volume=88 |issue=3 |pages=369–419 |url=https://match.pmf.kg.ac.rs/electronic_versions/Match89/n2/match89n2_371-388.pdf |doi=10.46793/match.89-2.371D}}</ref>

== Related concepts and generalizations ==

=== Total irregularity ===

A related measure, the '''total irregularity''', was introduced by Abdo, Brandt, and Dimitrov. It is defined as the sum of absolute degree differences over all pairs of vertices, not just adjacent ones:<ref name="abdo2014">{{cite journal |last1=Abdo |first1=Hosam |last2=Brandt |first2=Stephan |last3=Dimitrov |first3=Darko |title=The total irregularity of a graph |journal=Discrete Mathematics & Theoretical Computer Science |year=2014 |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=201–206 |doi=10.46298/dmtcs.1263 |url=https://dmtcs.episciences.org/1263/pdf|doi-access=free }}</ref>
:<math>\operatorname{irr}t(G) = \frac{1}{2}\sum{u,v \in V(G)} |\deg(u) - \deg(v)|</math>
Unlike the Albertson index, the total irregularity depends only on the [[degree sequence]] of a graph, not its specific edge structure.<ref name="abdo2014"/>

=== Generalized Albertson index ===

A generalization was introduced by Lin, Zhou, Wang, and Miao in 2022. The '''general Albertson index''' (or '''<math>p</math>-Albertson index''') is defined as:<ref name="lin2022">{{cite journal |last1=Lin |first1=Zhen |last2=Zhou |first2=Ting |last3=Wang |first3=Xiaojing |last4=Miao |first4=Lianying |title=The general Albertson irregularity index of graphs |journal=AIMS Mathematics |year=2022 |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=25–38 |doi=10.3934/math.2022002 |arxiv=
2107.06145}}</ref>
:<math>A_p(G) = \left(\sum_{uv \in E(G)} |\deg(u) - \deg(v)|^p\right)^{1/p}</math>
where <math>p</math> is a positive real number. This reduces to the classical Albertson index for <math>p = 1</math>. For <math>p = 2</math>, its square <math>A_2^2(G)</math> is known as the <math>\sigma</math>-index and is related to the [[Zagreb indices]] and the ''forgotten topological index''. The extremal trees for the <math>p</math>-Albertson index remain the path graph (minimum) and the star graph (maximum).<ref name="lin2022"/>

== Applications and connections ==

The Albertson index has applications in [[mathematical chemistry]] for predicting physicochemical properties of molecules in [[QSAR]]/[[QSPR]] modeling. In [[network science]], it provides a quantitative measure of network heterogeneity.

The concept is also connected to other graph theoretical topics, such as [[stepwise irregular graph]]s, where every edge has an imbalance of exactly 1,<ref name="gutman2018">{{cite journal |last=Gutman |first=Ivan |title=Stepwise irregular graphs |journal=Applied Mathematics and Computation |volume=325 |pages=234–238 |year=2018 |doi=10.1016/j.amc.2017.12.045}}</ref> and the [[imbalance conjecture]], which studies whether sequences of edge imbalances can form a valid [[degree sequence]] of some graph.<ref name="koz">{{cite journal |last1=Kozerenko |first1=Sergiy |last2=Skochko |first2=Volodymyr |title=On graphs with graphic imbalance sequences |journal=Algebra and Discrete Mathematics |date=2014 |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=97–108 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/289776294}}</ref>
